questions.stem: An architect is designing a review system for auto-generated infrastructure-as-code (IaC) templates. The templates are generated in 50-file batches. The team must choose between: Option X - one review instance that reads all 50 files in a single context, and Option Y - 50 parallel per-file instances followed by a cross-file consistency instance. Budget and time are constrained. Which option should the architect choose, and what is the most accurate reasoning?

options.A: Option X, because a single large context allows the reviewer to see all interdependencies simultaneously without coordination overhead
options.B: Option X, because multi-instance architectures always produce more false positives than single-instance review
options.C: Option Y, because per-file instances each operate at optimal context depth for local issues, and the cross-file instance receives structured summaries rather than 50 raw files, keeping both passes within effective context utilisation - while also parallelising Phase 1 to reduce wall-clock time
options.D: Option Y, because parallel per-file instances are always faster and cheaper than a single large-context review

questions.stem:
You are building a structured data extraction system using Claude. The system extracts information from unstructured documents, validates output using JSON schemas, and maintains high accuracy. It must handle edge cases gracefully and integrate with downstream systems.

Your nightly run submits 30,000 document extraction requests. The result processing job must update the correct downstream record for each successful extraction and resubmit only the documents that failed validation or exceeded context limits. During testing, engineers notice that relying on the result file's line order creates occasional mismatches after retries and partial failure handling. What design should you use?

options.A: Ask Claude to include the source filename in every extraction, then parse that field when processing failures.
options.B: Assign a stable custom_id derived from each document record, persist it with request metadata, and reconcile results using that identifier.
options.C: Assume batch results preserve submission order, then join each response to the original manifest by its array position.
options.D: Submit one combined request containing all documents, so every extraction and failure appears in a single ordered output.

questions.correct_option_text: Assign a stable custom_id derived from each document record, persist it with request metadata, and reconcile results using that identifier.
questions.explanation: The Message Batches API is designed around custom_id fields for correlating requests with responses. Each request must include a unique custom_id, and results are returned with matching custom_ids — not in submission order. The Anthropic docs state: 'A unique custom_id for identifying the Messages request.' Persisting this identifier with request metadata enables reliable reconciliation of successes and failures regardless of result ordering, retry interleaving, or partial failure handling.

explanation_citation.quote: A unique custom_id for identifying the Messages request. Must be 1 to 64 characters and contain only alphanumeric characters, hyphens, and underscores

A.text: Asking Claude to include source filenames in extraction output relies on the model to generate consistent identifiers and requires parsing that field — it is less reliable than a stable custom_id assigned by the calling application.
A.citation_quote: custom_id fields for correlating batch request/response pairs

C.text: Batch results are explicitly not guaranteed to preserve submission order. The Anthropic docs confirm results are returned per-request independently, not in array-position order. Relying on positional matching will produce mismatches after retries.
C.citation_quote: The batch is then processed asynchronously, with each request handled independently

D.text: Submitting all documents in one combined request is not how the Batches API works — each document must be a separate request in the batch with its own custom_id. A single combined request does not enable per-document result correlation.

Developer surveys indicate growing distrust-many have started dismissing findings without review because "half are wrong." The high false positive categories are undermining confidence in the accurate categories. What approach best restores developer trust while improving the system?

options.B: Temporarily disable high false positive categories (style, naming, documentation) and run only high-precision categories while improving prompts.

options.D: Apply a uniform strictness reduction across all categories to bring the overall false positive rate to an acceptable level.

questions.stem: A developer polls a batch status endpoint every 30 seconds to check whether their 10,000-request batch has finished. Batch processing takes around 4 hours on average. questions.stem: A financial auditing application feeds a 200-page annual report into Claude to identify discrepancies between the 'Management Discussion' section and the 'Financial Footnotes' section. Claude successfully identifies major thematic differences but consistently misses specific numerical contradictions. How should the architect redesign the system to catch these numerical issues?

options.A: The context window is exceeded, causing Claude to silently truncate the middle of the document; the document must be summarized before processing.
options.B: Implement a multi-pass review extracting relevant numerical claims locally from each section first, then comparing them in a separate cross-reference integration pass.
options.C: The application should use a separate Claude instance to generate the Financial Footnotes from scratch and compare them against the original document.
options.D: The prompt lacks a system message instructing Claude to act as an expert financial auditor, which lowers the baseline accuracy of numerical comparisons.

questions.correct_option_text: Implement a multi-pass review extracting relevant numerical claims locally from each section first, then comparing them in a separate cross-reference integration pass.
questions.explanation: Multi-pass review (per-section local extraction of numerical claims followed by a separate cross-reference pass) avoids attention dilution that occurs when one pass tries to do both fine-grained extraction and cross-section comparison on a 200-page document.

explanation_citation.quote: Multi-pass review: splitting large reviews into per-file local analysis passes plus cross-file integration passes to avoid attention dilution and contradictory findings

A.text: Claude does not silently truncate documents within its context window. The failure described - missing numerical contradictions - is consistent with attention dilution, not truncation; summarizing first would lose the precise figures needed for the comparison.
A.citation_quote: The "lost in the middle" effect: models reliably process information at the beginning and end of long inputs but may omit findings from middle sections

C.text: Regenerating the financial footnotes from scratch is a hallucination invitation; the source-of-truth document already exists. The documented approach is multi-pass review of the actual document.
C.citation_quote: Multi-pass review: splitting large reviews into per-file local analysis passes plus cross-file integration passes to avoid attention dilution and contradictory findings

D.text: Persona-style system prompts do not address the structural problem of asking one pass to do both extraction and cross-section comparison on a long document.
D.citation_quote: Multi-pass review: splitting large reviews into per-file local analysis passes plus cross-file integration passes to avoid attention dilution and contradictory findings

doc_reference.quote: Multi-pass review: splitting large reviews into per-file local analysis passes plus cross-file integration passes to avoid attention dilution and contradictory findings

questions.stem: You are designing a retry policy for an agentic pipeline. A senior engineer asks how many retries are considered safe before escalating. What is the recommended maximum number of retries before escalating or falling back when a tool call continues to fail?

options.A: Unlimited, until the model succeeds

questions.explanation: Documented guidance is that Claude will retry tool calls 2-3 times with corrections before giving up, which is also the recommended ceiling for a retry policy. Beyond that, escalate or fall back, since further retries waste cost and rarely resolve persistent failures.

explanation_citation.quote: If a tool request is invalid or missing parameters, Claude will retry 2-3 times with corrections before apologizing to the user.

A.text: Unlimited retries can burn through quota, mask underlying problems, and lock the agent in an unrecoverable state. The documented bound is 2-3 retries before escalation.
A.citation_quote: Claude will retry 2-3 times with corrections before apologizing to the user

B.text: A single retry is too restrictive: many transient failures resolve on the second or third attempt. The documented ceiling is 2-3, not 1.
B.citation_quote: Claude will retry 2-3 times with corrections before apologizing to the user

D.text: 5-10 retries exceed the documented bound and amplify cost and latency without proportional benefit; persistent failures should escalate well before that point.
D.citation_quote: Claude will retry 2-3 times with corrections before apologizing to the user

doc_reference.quote: If a tool request is invalid or missing parameters, Claude will retry 2-3 times with corrections before apologizing to the user.

questions.stem:
The code review component works iteratively: Claude analyzes a changed file, then may request related files (imports, base classes, tests) via tool calling to understand context before providing final feedback. Your application defines a tool that lets Claude request file contents; Claude invokes this tool, receives results, and continues its analysis. You're evaluating batch processing to reduce API costs.
What is the primary technical constraint when considering batch processing for this workflow?

options.A: The batch API doesn't support tool definitions in request parameters.
options.B: The asynchronous model prevents executing tools mid-request and returning results for Claude to continue analysis.
options.C: Batch processing lacks request correlation identifiers for matching outputs to input requests.
options.D: Batch processing latency of up to 24 hours is too slow for pull request feedback, though the workflow could otherwise function.

questions.correct_option_text: The asynchronous model prevents executing tools mid-request and returning results for Claude to continue analysis.
questions.explanation: The Message Batches API is asynchronous and processes each request independently; it cannot pause mid-request to execute a client-side tool and feed the result back. That breaks the iterative tool-calling pattern the review workflow relies on, regardless of latency.

explanation_citation.quote: The batch API does not support multi-turn tool calling within a single request (cannot execute tools mid-request and return results)

A.text: Batch requests can include tool definitions; the constraint is on multi-turn tool execution mid-request, not on declaring tools.
A.citation_quote: What can be batched: Vision, Tool use, System messages, Multi-turn conversations, Any beta features

C.text: Batch processing supports request correlation via custom_id, so this is the opposite of documented behavior.
C.citation_quote: A unique custom_id for identifying the Messages request.

D.text: Latency is a real downside, but it isn't the primary technical blocker: even if it ran instantly, batch can't drive the mid-request tool loop the review needs.
D.citation_quote: The batch API does not support multi-turn tool calling within a single request (cannot execute tools mid-request and return results)

doc_reference.quote: The batch API does not support multi-turn tool calling within a single request (cannot execute tools mid-request and return results)

questions.stem: An architect is designing a tool schema for extracting product data. Some products have a `discount_percent` field and some do not. The team debates whether to mark the field `required` or to allow it to be absent. What is the recommended approach for optional fields in a tool `input_schema` to prevent Claude from hallucinating values?

options.A: Omit the field from the schema entirely so Claude never knows it exists
options.B: Add the field to `required` and tell Claude in the system prompt to skip it when unknown
options.C: Include the field in `required` and set a default value of `0` in the description
options.D: List the field in `properties` but exclude it from the `required` array, and allow `null` via a type union or `nullable` flag

questions.correct_option_text: List the field in `properties` but exclude it from the `required` array, and allow `null` via a type union or `nullable` flag
questions.explanation: When source documents may not contain a value, the field should be in properties but excluded from required, with null permitted (type union or nullable). This prevents the model from fabricating values just to satisfy a required field. Marking a field required forces the model to produce something even when the information is absent, which drives hallucinations in extraction.

explanation_citation.quote: Designing schema fields as optional (nullable) when source documents may not contain the information, preventing the model from fabricating values to satisfy required fields

A.text: Omitting the field hides legitimate values when they do exist. The field should be in the schema so the model can populate it when present and leave it null when absent.
A.citation_quote: Designing schema fields as optional (nullable) when source documents may not contain the information, preventing the model from fabricating values to satisfy required fields

B.text: Required + a prompt instruction to skip is the exact failure mode the guide warns against: prompt-only guidance is probabilistic, while the schema still demands a value, so the model fabricates rather than skips.
B.citation_quote: When deterministic compliance is required (e.g., identity verification before financial operations), prompt instructions alone have a non-zero failure rate

C.text: Defaulting a missing percent to 0 silently mislabels absent data as a real 0% discount. The recommended pattern is to keep the field optional/nullable so absence is preserved.
C.citation_quote: Designing schema fields as optional (nullable) when source documents may not contain the information, preventing the model from fabricating values to satisfy required fields

doc_reference.quote: Designing schema fields as optional (nullable) when source documents may not contain the information, preventing the model from fabricating values to satisfy required fields

questions.stem:
You are building a structured data extraction system using Claude. The system extracts information from unstructured documents, validates output using JSON schemas, and maintains high accuracy. It must handle edge cases gracefully and integrate with downstream systems.

Production review shows inconsistent routing: documents with unreadable required values and unfamiliar layouts sometimes flow into downstream systems, while routine invoices missing optional purchase-order numbers are sent for manual review. The extraction schema already permits nullable fields for data that is absent from the source. What change would most effectively improve routing decisions?

options.A: Require retries until all schema fields are populated, then escalate only documents still containing null values.
options.B: Add explicit human-review criteria with few-shot examples distinguishing absent optional fields, unreadable required fields, and unsupported document types.
options.C: Escalate documents based on frustrated wording, urgent language, or negative sentiment detected in the source text.
options.D: Route documents to reviewers whenever the model reports confidence below a single global threshold after extraction.

questions.correct_option_text: Add explicit human-review criteria with few-shot examples distinguishing absent optional fields, unreadable required fields, and unsupported document types.
questions.explanation: Inconsistent routing stems from unclear decision boundaries: the system treats absent optional fields the same as unreadable required fields, and doesn't distinguish unsupported document layouts. Adding explicit human-review criteria with few-shot examples for each routing case teaches the model when to proceed versus escalate. The exam guide identifies few-shot examples as especially effective for ambiguous routing cases where similar-looking documents require different outcomes.

explanation_citation.quote: Adding explicit escalation criteria with few-shot examples to the system prompt demonstrating when to escalate versus resolve autonomously

A.text: Requiring retries until all fields are populated forces fabrication for genuinely absent optional fields, and escalating any remaining nulls still doesn't distinguish between null-because-absent and null-because-unreadable.
A.citation_quote: Designing schema fields as optional (nullable) when source documents may not contain the information, preventing the model from fabricating values to satisfy required fields

C.text: Sentiment detection is an unreliable proxy for document routing; the exam guide warns that sentiment-based escalation is not a reliable signal for actual processing complexity or error type.
C.citation_quote: Why sentiment-based escalation and self-reported confidence scores are unreliable proxies for actual case complexity

D.text: A single global confidence threshold ignores that confidence is miscalibrated differently across document families and field types, exactly the segmentation problem the exam guide warns about.
D.citation_quote: The risk that aggregate accuracy metrics [...] may mask poor performance on specific document types or fields

questions.stem: A large organization uses Claude for dozens of different extraction tasks, from processing HR forms to legal documents. They are building a central feedback database where user corrections are stored to generate few-shot examples for prompt improvement. The database stores the original text, the model's incorrect output, and the user's corrected output. What additional piece of metadata is most critical to include in each database entry to make this feedback loop effective at scale?

options.A: The latency of the model's original response, to correlate errors with performance.
options.B: The specific prompt or task identifier (e.g., 'InvoiceExtractionV2'), to ensure corrections are used to build few-shot sets only for the relevant task.
options.C: The username of the person who made the correction, for auditing purposes.
options.D: The timestamp of the correction, to track improvement over time.

questions.correct_option_text: The specific prompt or task identifier (e.g., 'InvoiceExtractionV2'), to ensure corrections are used to build few-shot sets only for the relevant task.
questions.explanation: Task 4.4's feedback-loop guidance is to track which patterns trigger findings so corrections can be analyzed and reused per task. With dozens of extraction tasks, corrections must be tagged with a task identifier so few-shot sets are built only from the relevant task's history; without the task identifier, corrections from one extraction would contaminate another.

explanation_citation.quote: Feedback loop design: tracking which code constructs trigger findings (detected_pattern field) to enable systematic analysis of dismissal patterns

A.text: Latency is performance metadata; it doesn't help build correctly scoped few-shot sets and isn't tied to which corrections apply to which task.
A.citation_quote: Feedback loop design: tracking which code constructs trigger findings

C.text: Auditor identity is useful for governance but not for routing corrections to the right prompt; without the task ID, the corrections still mix across tasks.
C.citation_quote: Feedback loop design: tracking which code constructs trigger findings

D.text: Timestamps support trend analysis but not task scoping; you can still mis-attribute a correction to the wrong extraction without a task identifier.
D.citation_quote: Feedback loop design: tracking which code constructs trigger findings

doc_reference.quote: Feedback loop design: tracking which code constructs trigger findings (detected_pattern field) to enable systematic analysis of dismissal patterns

questions.stem: A customer service bot uses tool_choice: {"type": "auto"} with a log_complaint tool. When users send long, detailed emails, the bot successfully calls the tool. However, when users send short messages like "Fix my billing!", the bot often replies with conversational text (e.g., "I understand you're frustrated, I will log this") instead of calling the tool. You want to force the bot to always log the complaint via the tool, regardless of message length. What is the correct configuration?

options.A: Add a second tool called log_short_complaint .
options.B: Increase the temperature parameter to 1.0.
options.C: Add a system prompt telling Claude to be less empathetic.
options.D: Change tool_choice to {"type": "any"} .

questions.correct_option_text: Change tool_choice to {"type": "any"} .
questions.explanation: tool_choice: {"type": "any"} forces the model to call one of the provided tools instead of returning conversational text. That's exactly the documented use case: when the agent sometimes replies with empathetic prose instead of calling log_complaint, switching from auto to any guarantees a tool call regardless of message length.

explanation_citation.quote: Setting tool_choice: 'any' to guarantee the model calls a tool rather than returning conversational text

A.text: Adding a second tool doesn't fix the underlying issue (model preferring text over tool); it just gives the model another option to ignore. The documented fix is forcing tool use, not adding more tools.
A.citation_quote: tool_choice: 'any' to guarantee the model calls a tool rather than returning conversational text

B.text: Higher temperature increases variance but doesn't address the auto/any decision boundary; the model can still choose to respond conversationally, just with more variability.
B.citation_quote: tool_choice: 'any' to guarantee the model calls a tool

C.text: Prompt-level instructions to be less empathetic don't guarantee tool invocation and create a worse user experience; the tool_choice mechanism is the documented enforcement primitive.
C.citation_quote: tool_choice: 'any' to guarantee the model calls a tool rather than returning conversational text

doc_reference.quote: Setting tool_choice: 'any' to guarantee the model calls a tool rather than returning conversational text

questions.stem: An orchestrator detects that Claude has called the same tool with identical arguments three consecutive times without success. What mechanism should an orchestrator maintain to detect and break potential infinite retry loops?

options.A: A detected_pattern tracker that records repeated tool calls and their arguments
options.B: Disabling all tools after the first failure
options.C: Increasing the temperature of Claude's sampler after each retry
options.D: A hard-coded sleep of 5 seconds between retries

questions.correct_option_text: A detected_pattern tracker that records repeated tool calls and their arguments
questions.explanation: An orchestrator should track repeated tool invocations and their argument patterns so it can detect when the same call is being retried unsuccessfully. A detected_pattern tracker records this signal, allowing the loop to break out (or escalate) once a threshold of identical-argument retries is reached, preventing wasted iterations.

explanation_citation.quote: Feedback loop design: tracking which code constructs trigger findings (detected_pattern field) to enable systematic analysis of dismissal patterns

B.text: Disabling all tools after a single failure is far too aggressive; many tool failures are transient or arg-specific. The orchestrator should detect repeated identical retries, not blanket-disable on first error.
B.citation_quote: Feedback loop design: tracking which code constructs trigger findings (detected_pattern field) to enable systematic analysis of dismissal patterns

C.text: Raising sampler temperature does not detect or break loops; it only diversifies generations. The control-flow problem is structural and needs an orchestrator-level tracker.
C.citation_quote: Feedback loop design: tracking which code constructs trigger findings (detected_pattern field) to enable systematic analysis of dismissal patterns

D.text: A fixed sleep slows retries but does not detect the loop or stop it; the agent will still issue the same identical call indefinitely. Loop detection requires state, not delay.
D.citation_quote: Feedback loop design: tracking which code constructs trigger findings (detected_pattern field) to enable systematic analysis of dismissal patterns

questions.stem: A legal tech startup is building a contract analysis tool. Users upload contracts through a web interface and expect a summary within 10 seconds. The startup also runs a monthly analysis on all contracts uploaded that month to generate macro-trends for an internal dashboard. Which API strategy best balances cost and user experience?

options.A: Use the Batch API for user uploads and the synchronous API for the monthly analysis.
options.B: Use the Batch API for both workloads to maximize the 50% cost savings.
options.C: Use the synchronous API for user uploads and the Batch API for the monthly analysis.
options.D: Use the synchronous API for both workloads to simplify the system architecture and reduce maintenance.

questions.correct_option_text: Use the synchronous API for user uploads and the Batch API for the monthly analysis.
questions.explanation: The two workloads have opposite latency profiles. User uploads are interactive with a 10-second budget, which only the synchronous API meets. The monthly aggregate analysis is non-interactive and tolerates the batch SLA, where Batch API earns the cost discount. Mapping API approach to latency requirement is the documented decision rule.

explanation_citation.quote: Matching API approach to workflow latency requirements: synchronous API for blocking pre-merge checks, batch API for overnight/weekly analysis

A.text: This swaps the two: it puts user-facing 10-second uploads on the high-latency Batch API and pays full price for non-urgent monthly analysis. It maximizes user pain while sacrificing the batch discount where it matters.
A.citation_quote: Matching API approach to workflow latency requirements: synchronous API for blocking pre-merge checks, batch API for overnight/weekly analysis

B.text: Routing user uploads through the Batch API breaks the 10-second SLA that the interactive UI requires. Cost savings are not worth violating the latency contract.
B.citation_quote: Matching API approach to workflow latency requirements: synchronous API for blocking pre-merge checks, batch API for overnight/weekly analysis

D.text: Using the synchronous API for the monthly batch job pays full price for work that has no latency requirement, leaving the documented batch discount on the table.
D.citation_quote: Matching API approach to workflow latency requirements: synchronous API for blocking pre-merge checks, batch API for overnight/weekly analysis

questions.stem: An architect builds an agent that must handle both simple lookups (e.g., 'What is the status of order #1234?') and complex investigations (e.g., 'Why was order #1234 delayed and what is the impact on the customer's account?'). Currently both types use the same processing pipeline with extended thinking, making simple lookups slow. What architecture balances speed and depth?

options.A: Use a classifier to route simple lookups (effort='low', no thinking) to a fast path and complex investigations (effort='high', thinking enabled) to a deep-analysis path
options.B: Disable extended thinking for all requests and rely on tool results for complex analysis
options.C: Let users select 'quick' or 'detailed' mode for their queries
options.D: Add a timeout that kills thinking after 3 seconds for simple queries

questions.correct_option_text: Use a classifier to route simple lookups (effort='low', no thinking) to a fast path and complex investigations (effort='high', thinking enabled) to a deep-analysis path
questions.explanation: Coordinators should analyze query requirements and dynamically select the right path rather than always routing through the full pipeline. A classifier that sends simple lookups to a low-effort, no-thinking path and complex investigations to a high-effort path with thinking enabled balances latency and depth, applying expensive reasoning only where the query benefits from it.

explanation_citation.quote: Designing coordinator agents that analyze query requirements and dynamically select which subagents to invoke rather than always routing through the full pipeline

B.text: Disabling extended thinking everywhere removes the depth needed for genuinely complex investigations. The right pattern is conditional routing, not blanket removal.
B.citation_quote: Designing coordinator agents that analyze query requirements and dynamically select which subagents to invoke

C.text: User-selected modes shift judgment to humans who often cannot tell which path their query needs, and they don't address the underlying architecture. Programmatic routing based on query features is more reliable.
C.citation_quote: Designing coordinator agents that analyze query requirements and dynamically select which subagents to invoke

D.text: A 3-second timeout on extended thinking is an arbitrary cutoff that may truncate useful reasoning or still incur the start-up cost. The documented pattern is to skip thinking for low-effort queries entirely, not interrupt it mid-stream.

doc_reference.quote: Designing coordinator agents that analyze query requirements and dynamically select which subagents to invoke rather than always routing through the full pipeline

questions.stem: An architect is designing a schema to extract the contract_effective_date from legal agreements. The agreements often have one date on the first page and a different date in the signature block. The schema includes page_1_date, signature_date, and a conflict_detected boolean. What is the most critical prompt engineering technique to ensure the model accurately populates the conflict_detected boolean?

options.A: Use a high temperature setting so the model is more likely to notice subtle differences between the dates.
options.B: Instruct the model to extract both dates first, and then explicitly compare them in a <scratchpad> before setting the boolean value.
options.C: Instruct the model to evaluate the boolean first, before extracting the dates, to establish the logical flow.
options.D: Provide a few-shot example where the dates match perfectly, so the model knows what a non-conflict looks like.

questions.correct_option_text: Instruct the model to extract both dates first, and then explicitly compare them in a <scratchpad> before setting the boolean value.
questions.explanation: To populate conflict_detected accurately, the model must first extract both candidate dates and then explicitly compare them in a scratchpad before setting the boolean. This step-by-step reasoning pattern (chain-of-thought) is exactly the self-correction validation flow recommended for conflict_detected booleans.

explanation_citation.quote: Designing self-correction validation flows: extracting "calculated_total" alongside "stated_total" to flag discrepancies, adding "conflict_detected" booleans for inconsistent source data

A.text: Higher temperature increases output variance, not factual accuracy on extraction tasks. Anthropic's guidance for deterministic extraction is to lower, not raise, temperature.

C.text: Setting the boolean before extracting the dates inverts the required dependency: you cannot detect a conflict between values you have not yet extracted. Reasoning must precede the conclusion.
C.citation_quote: Manual CoT as a fallback. When thinking is off, you can still encourage step-by-step reasoning by asking Claude to think through the problem. Use structured tags like `<thinking>` and `<answer>` to cleanly separate reasoning from the final output.

D.text: Few-shot examples should cover edge cases, including conflicts; showing only matching dates teaches the model to expect agreement and miss real conflicts.
D.citation_quote: Diverse: Cover edge cases and vary enough that Claude doesn't pick up unintended patterns.

doc_reference.quote: Designing self-correction validation flows: extracting "calculated_total" alongside "stated_total" to flag discrepancies, adding "conflict_detected" booleans for inconsistent source data
